ruach is rendered 'wind' in both layers (STEPBible 'a wind', all five English versions 'wind'). The echo of the 'ruach of God' over the waters in Gen 1:2 is my own reading, not a claim from the packet commentaries; the commentary flags it as such.

STEPBible glosses vayyachel as 'and he waited' (root yachal/chul). Rashi and Radak read it as a hiphil of chul 'to wait'. Ibn Ezra finds the form odd. I followed the waiting sense; the Niphal-form in 8:12 (vayyiyachel) is discussed in the commentary there.

Rashi's remark that the dove here is masculine (taraf) and Ramban's rejection of it are summarised in the notes; the English keeps 'she' as in the other versions. The midrash on the bitter olive (Rashi, Radak, Ramban citing Genesis Rabbah) is reported as the commentators' reading, not mine. The mention of 'Genesis Rabbah' comes only from Ramban's and Radak's text in the packet.

The 'first month' is disputed in the commentaries: Rashi gives R. Eliezer (Tishri) against R. Joshua (Nisan); Radak takes Tishri. I left the month unnamed in the translation and mention the dispute only in the commentary. The packet's event dating is the chronologist's, not mine.

The Hebrew uses two different verbs, ḥārēb (v13, twice) and yābēš (v14). All five English versions blur them into 'dried/dry'. I kept them apart: ḥārēb is 'dry out' in the glosses and 'dry' in the literal layer of v13, yābēš is 'be dry' in v14, and the commentary explains the difference, following Rashi and Radak, who read ḥārēb as a surface crust over mud.

Day count: 7:11 puts the flood's start on the 17th of the second month in Noah's 600th year, and v14 is the 27th of the second month a year later, so one year and ten days by a solar count. Rashi and Radak explain the ten/eleven days as the surplus of the solar over the lunar year; this is rabbinic harmonization and I flag it as such in the commentary.

Ketiv hōṣē' (written הוצא) against Qere hayṣē' (read הַיְצֵא). Both are Hiphil imperatives 'bring out'; the Qere has the regular y- of the root. Rashi's midrashic split (Ketiv: bring them out yourself; Qere: tell them to go out) is reported but not adopted. I glossed the Qere as the packet shows it.
mišpəḥōt 'families' is rendered 'families' in both layers, not 'kinds'. KJV's 'after their kinds' harmonizes with min in Genesis 1; here the Hebrew word is the one used of human clans.

The conjunction kî before 'the inclination of the human heart is evil' can be causal ('for', KJV/ASV), concessive ('though', YLT and many modern versions) or explanatory. Ramban reads it as mitigating (youth, not age), which favors the concessive sense. I kept 'for' in the literal layer and used 'even though' in the dramatic layer.

Ancient Near Eastern comparison (Gilgamesh XI: after the sacrifice the gods smell the savor and gather like flies) is from my own knowledge, not from the packet; I left sources empty and described it generally.

The packet has no source for the claim that the six paired terms are two merisms of seasons plus day/night; that is my own structural reading. The rabbinic month-by-month assignment (Rashi) is cited as such.

The commentators disagree sharply on when the 150 days begin and how the months count (Rashi, Ibn Ezra, Ramban, Radak); I did not adjudicate and report only that the dating is disputed. Month and day numbers in the verse text are given as in the Hebrew.
Noach / tanach / manoach (8:9) share the root nwh. I treat the sound play as real but do not claim an intent; no packet commentary names it.

The Hebrew says only that the raven 'went out, going out and returning' (yatzo vashov); it does not say it came back to the ark. Rashi reads circling the ark; Radak reads going to and from its nest; Sforno reads that it could not endure the air. The five English versions all say 'to and fro'. I kept the ambiguity in the literal layer.
